hints: Focus on what X and Y must be, since an ester with conc. H2SO4 is always made from a carboxylic acid plus an alcohol.
Remember that NaBH4 reduces the aldehyde CH3(CH2)2CHO to its primary alcohol, butan-1-ol, CH3(CH2)2CH2OH.
Now pair that alcohol with the oxidation product from Cr2O7 2-/H+ and join them as acid-CO2-alcohol to count the carbons on each side.
walkthrough:
**Identify X from reduction**

NaBH4 is a reducing agent. It adds hydrogen to an aldehyde to give a primary alcohol with the same carbon skeleton.

$$\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_2\text{CHO} + 2[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$$
So X is butan-1-ol.

**Identify Y from oxidation**

Acidified dichromate, $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}/\text{H}^+$, is a strong oxidising agent. It oxidises an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid with the same number of carbons.

$$\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_2\text{CHO} + [\text{O}] \rightarrow \text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$$
So Y is butanoic acid.

**Form the ester**

Carboxylic acid + alcohol with conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ gives ester + water. The acid provides the $\text{CO}_2$ part and the alcohol provides the O-alkyl part.

$$\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_2\text{CO}_2\text{H} + \text{HO}(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{CH}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_2\text{CO}_2(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
This is butyl butanoate, the pineapple aroma ester.

options.A: This is propyl butanoate. The acid side is correct as butanoate, but the alcohol side is one carbon too short. It assumes X was propan-1-ol instead of butan-1-ol from reduction of butanal.
options.B: This is butyl butanoate, CH3(CH2)2CO2(CH2)3CH3. Y is butanoic acid giving the CH3(CH2)2CO2 part, and X is butan-1-ol giving the O(CH2)3CH3 part. Esterification joins them correctly.
options.C: This swaps the chain lengths the wrong way. It suggests a 5-carbon acid with a 3-carbon alcohol, which cannot come from a 4-carbon starting aldehyde by simple reduction and oxidation.
options.D: This is butyl pentanoate. Both sides are one carbon too long. It is the trap if you think oxidation of an aldehyde adds a carbon, or you miscount CH3(CH2)2CHO as a 5-carbon molecule.
